speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by the thousands, Canadians have expressed their shock and dismay about the proposed cuts in environmental and wildlife research activities. Highly trained biologists, zoologists, and specialists in a variety of disciplines, are about to lose their jobs. Their only prospects seem to be south of the border because provincial Governments are not prepared to absorb them, nor is the private sector.
A better understanding of the role of wildlife in the ecosystem is an essential and never ending process. The Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) must understand that wildlife research and activities mean more than human health. In addition, the announced cuts have dealt a heavy blow to the morale of people within her Department. She must fight for the preservation of the Canadian Wildlife Service at its present strength before the announcement of cuts.
Today, in a letter by author Farley Mowat and the President of the Public Service of Canada, Jack Donegani, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), they urge him to reconsider the cuts in the Canadian Wildlife Service. We on this side of the House again urge the Minister of the Environment to fight for the Canadian Wildlife Service, reject the cuts, and restore confidence in her Department, by her employees-
I must inform the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has made it quite clear that the rationale behind all the cut-backs and tax increases in his economic statement is to increase investor confidence in Canada.
The Canadian investment community has now had ample opportunity to witness the new Government in operation and to assess its supposedly new approach to our economic problems. Has it responded like the Government suggested they would? Has it suddenly found renewed faith in the Canadian economy and begun to invest, and produce the tens upon tens of thousands of jobs that we were promised would be created overnight? The answer is clear, and it is no.
Just last week, for example, Great Lakes Forest Products Limited of Thunder Bay announced that it will be investing $25 million to build a newsprint mill in the United States because it has more confidence in the American economy than in Canada's. Today's Globe and Mail indicated that production and employment by Canadian manufacturers have taken a sharp drop. A spokesman is quoted as saying: "There sure seems to be a lack of confidence".
The Government's approach is not working because it is based on faulty assumptions. Just wanting increased investor confidence is not enough. We need concrete actions to put Canadians back to work. It is obvious that Canadian investors, as well as the Canadian public, do not have faith in the Conservative Government's approach. They do not believe, as I do not believe, that the Conservatives have any answers. Not only is the Government's honeymoon just about over, but it appears that most Canadians are ready to sue for divorce.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to express the satisfaction of my constituents in the riding of Beauce and that of all Canadians with respect to the positive attitude taken by the Canadian Government in providing aid to Ethiopia.
Our Government's initiative was instrumental in persuading other countries, agencies and thousands of Canadians to make a generous contribution.
Mr. Speaker, everyone understands that we should help people who are starving and many of whom are actually dying of starvation. However, I think our own attitude in this country is entirely ambiguous, in that we are not prepared to protect the right to life of defenceless creatures. This is a shameful injustice, Mr. Speaker.

December 5, 1984
We do not want to let old people, men, women and children die in Ethiopia, and our actions are laudable. But why do we let our own children be killed, in a civilized country?
We are willing to protect and to help people in need, but why do we let our own children be killed by abortionists who operate freely without any scruples?
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as a Member of this House, 1 still fail to understand how we can make such admirable efforts to feed the hungry of the world and at the same time let others kill those who have a right to be born.

Mr. Speaker, at the time when the Government is attempting to lead the way in curbing excessive government spending as a result of the economic mess this Party inherited from the Liberals, 1 want to point out a situation I discovered within the Bank of Canada.
Currently the Ottawa office of the Bank of Canada operates a cafeteria which offers employees heavily subsidized meals. For example, from yesterday's menu patrons could order beef short ribs for 80 cents, or tuna casserole for 65 cents. Milk sells for 20 cents. A side order of vegetables or rice is 15 cents, and soft drinks are 10 cents. I support your move, Mr. Speaker, to raise prices in our restaurants and cafeterias on the Hill, and I strongly urge the Governor of the Bank of Canada to do the same. The Bank of Canada should be setting an example, not breaking the bank at the taxpayers' expense.

Mr. Speaker, it has been brought to my attention that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is putting on an elaborate display today relating to all of its major activities on the pure science side, in the applied science areas, as well as information relating to the Candu reactor and, even more important, to the little known and numerous achievements that nuclear research has attained in the field of medical science. This display and public relations effort will take place at Atomic Energy of Canada Headquarters here in Ottawa, and only the Progressive Conservative Members of the House of Commons have been invited to participate.
I cannot emphasize enough the importance that the Conservative Members of the House of Commons should give to this very vital and key project in the field of the pure and applied sciences. I would impress upon each and every one of them that they should take the opportunity to attend and get
the real side of the story about this great achievement in the scientific history of Canada. I have been given to understand that a similar, future display will be presented for the Liberal caucus Members and one for the NDP caucus Members.
Some Canadians do not place enough emphasis on the outstanding, positive achievements of the many brilliant and dedicated expert personnel that we have in our country. The time is long overdue when the positive side of nuclear research must be accurately, spontaneously, and credibly placed on the record for all to see, not only in our own country where we sometimes give our own people the least credit for achievement, but also-
I would like to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I appeared before an interdepartmental hearing on auto emission standards to urge them to recommend the implementation of lower, less polluting auto emission standards for this country. Reducing auto emissions to at least the American level would be a step in the right direction, not only in reducing acid rain but also in enabling us to get tough with the Americans with respect to their massive contribution to acid rain. Reducing Canadian automobile emissions would help restore the credibility on this issue that was lost through previous Liberal inaction in this area.
The Government must also act in those areas where it itself has damaged the ability of Canada to advocate with integrity that the Americans be more sensitive to acid rain and other environmental problems; by re-instating the herring gull egg program which monitors toxins in the Great Lakes, and by reversing cuts in wildlife services, some of which affect international agreements and concerns like the future of the porcupine caribou herd in the Yukon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Trois-Rivieres riding which I have the honour to represent in the House is one of those that have been affected by the notorious and dismal affair of the Laprade Fund. I use the expression "dismal affair" because the previous government never fulfilled its commitments in this regard. We all know
December 5, 1984

that the money earmarked for the Laprade plant project that never materialized was supposed to be spent in the affected ridings to create permanent jobs, mostly in the energy sector.
Mr. Speaker, the previous government, not content with failing to fulfil its promises, made a farce out of the Laprade Fund by distributing right and left, here and there and everywhere in a wanton fashion subsidies which have never created permanent jobs of any sort.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot find words strong enough to describe the stupidity of the previous government in this affair, and my constituents are well aware that the members of that government are now trying to wash their hands of the whole mess as they sit on benches opposite. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that for my constituents it is better that way.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are law-abiding people and expect our courts and juries to uphold the law of the land. Yet in Toronto a jury acquitted Dr. Morgentaler, who admitted he broke Canada's laws and would continue to do so. A father who breaks the law by stealing bread to feed his hungry children is sent to jail, but in this case we have a jury acquitting a man who denies life to unborn babies. The fact that he has broken the law many times should not now make it right and proper. These juries are saying: "Break the law often and it is okay". If one believes the law is wrong, he has every right to work for a change but, until it is changed, it should be obeyed. Any other philosophy will bring chaos to the country.
Morgentaler's lawyer appears to justify breaking the law by saying: "... the right to control one's body is essential.. . ". Right on, Mr. Lawyer, but that control should happen before the act of intercourse, not by killing the child after he or she is conceived. I congratulate the Government of Ontario for appealing this case, and I hope the appeal court makes it abundantly clear that the laws of Canada must be obeyed by all, including Dr. Morgentaler.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 would borrow a phrase from President Reagan by saying that we will soon be able to consign those kinds of dinosaurs to the ash bin of history.

Oral Questions

I rise today to tell the House that the rebuilding of the Liberal Party of Canada has already begun under our most distinguished and right hon. Leader (Mr. Turner). On Monday a major poll conducted by Eastcan Research of Halifax was released and showed that the Liberal Party of Newfoundland now stands at 48 per cent in the polls while the governing Tories stand at 42 per cent. This poll shows what Newfoundlanders think of the Tory way of doing things, both in the Province of Newfoundland and here in Ottawa. Newfoundlanders and Labradorians have recognized the age-old maxim of our grandfathers: Tory times are indeed hard times.
May I offer a word of advice to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)? He should listen less to the applause of the mindless 211 cheerleaders he brought with him to the House of Commons, and pay more attention to the voices of the people of Canada who are upset at the double-cross that was perpetrated on them by a Prime Minister who promised compassion and gave them a cold shoulder, who promised to listen and gave them a closed door, and who paraded himself as the voice of ordinary Canadians, but who, in only a few months, has forgotten where those Canadians live and who they are.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I would like to address my question to the Prime Minister, who has just entered the House. I am tempted to note that the Minister of Finance is so afraid of losing his briefs that he is costing the Canadian taxpayers their shirts.
He confirmed in the House yesterday that we would see interest rates of 6.5 per cent. At the same time, in the same week, he authorized a long-term 20-year bond issue at 12 per cent that will cost Canadian taxpayers millions and millions of unnecessary dollars, if his forecast is correct.
How can the Government instil the sense of investor confidence in the private sector that it seeks if it issues a forecast which is completely imcompatible with the bond issue authorized earlier this week?

Mr. Speaker, I think that this Government instills a sense of confidence, in the markets and elsewhere, by bringing the first degree of sanity into the public finances of the country that we have seen in a long, long time.

Hear, hear!

December 5, 1984
Oral Questions

One of the major offenders who sent out conflicting signals was my hon. friend when he was running for the leadership of his own Party. He contradicted official government policy. He confused a lot of people, including the delegates to the Liberal leadership convention-but not enough.
The policies of economic renewal and growth which have been set out by the new Government and by the Minister of Finance are the stuff which will inspire sound decisions and will bring back a positive investment climate which will create jobs in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that's no answer; it is more bafflegab of the kind we got yesterday from the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my supplementary question to the Minister of State for Finance. If there are anticipated declines in interest rates, there are ways of managing the public debt under those circumstances. Undoubtedly the Minister has heard of, or perhaps considered, indexed bonds. Why does the Government not take this opportunity to cancel the issue that was proposed this week, go back to the drawing board and come up with a flexible instrument which will send a positive signal to the private sector and will result in the saving of millions and millions of dollars for Canadian taxpayers?
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to answer the Hon. Member's question. 1 recall a time when the former Government issued Canada Savings Bonds at 19 per cent.
Hear, hear!

We have no intention of cancelling the issue. It was appropriately priced and placed in the market. We are thoughtful when we put these issues together. As the Minister of Finance has suggested, our intent is for interest rates to come down under our administration. That has been a long time coming because of the former Government's record.

Mr. Speaker, I would hope that we are not going to see Ministers indulging in political arithmetic, because political arithmetic is exactly what she has just indulged in.
Is the Minister really not saying that the economic forecast was not credible, that the interest rate forecast was not credible, and that the deficit forecast was not credible? In short, is she not saying that the entire economic program as announced in the mini Budget of November 8 is not credible?

Mr. Speaker, I know that many of my hon. colleagues in this House agree that indeed, the economic statement was credible. Canadian people believe it is credible. I am sorry that the Hon. Member is having difficulty finding it credible.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. It concerns the November survey of the purchasing managers of Canada which shows the sharpest drop in production and employment which we have seen in the last two years. A spokesman for their association said in reference to the business community: "There sure seems to be a lack of confidence". Because of the shocking results of the survey which show this drop in production and employment, is the Minister now prepared to recommend to Cabinet a change of the policy of spending cuts and tax increases which, obviously up to this stage, has not worked?

Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with the Hon. Member that the measures we have proposed are not working, and will not work. This is a very small survey. 1 believe there were some 200 firms involved. As the Hon. Member knows, there are any number of surveys coming up, with any number of conclusions. Our forecasts indicate, and our information is that confidence is increasing in this country, and will continue to do so.
[ Translation]

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker.
Since business has already lost confidence in this Government's economic policies, what other measures does the Government intend to take in order to turn this trend around, if it remains as it is now?

Mr. Speaker, this Government is working every day toward rebuilding confidence and employment. I might point out to the Hon. Member that, even in the survey from which he quoted, production had increased by 23 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. As the Prime Minister knows, on November 8 his Government cancelled the summer employment program for students, which represents a cut of $85 million in the Summer Canada Program. He should also know that in only four months, approximately on April 15, the students of Canada will be on the streets and available for work.
Oral Questions
Many students are already looking for summer employment. Many of them are wondering how they are going to pay for next year's tuition. Will the Prime Minister assure this House that if he has any alternative program for summer employment-if he has one-he will do as was done in other years, and announce that program before this House adjourns on December 21 ?
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has already assured the Hon. Member, and through him, the House, that the programs of the previous Government in this area were unworkable-
Oh, oh!

-and considered as such by all Canadians, including the students of Canada who passed judgment on them along with the rest of the country, on September 4. We will have in place appropriate and helpful programs to deal with the requirements of students, in advance of next summer, by a long shot.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Hon. Secretary of State whose responsibility includes student loans. He has just heard that the Conservative Government still has no program in place for employment this summer that the students know about. He also knows that 94 per cent of post-secondary graduates hold down jobs.
Can he tell us why the Government has frozen $5 million which is used for student loans, and taken a route which will most certainly add to youth unemployment instead of reducing it? Is the money going to be saved on the backs of our youth?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague will know that there is division of opinion amongst Canadian students regarding the relative importance of additional financial support for student loans, and of incentive to create jobs. The students are concerned almost to a person that there be jobs available when they are finished university. Therefore, the result was a decision by this Government to focus on job creation and at the same time, as he
knows, the assistance to students under the Canada Student Loans Program was increased by this House last year.

Mr. Speaker, how can the Minister sit in submissive silence while the Government freezes this additional grant of $5 million, and at the same time it plunks down $220,000 for the education of political aides? Is the education of political commissars more important than the education of young people to get a job?
Ask Lloyd Axworthy.
Mine were already trained when I got them.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member chooses to ignore the adjustments in assistance to the students which were made during the last period of time. He also chooses to ignore the fact that it was his Party which imposed six and five on the entire university community and brought about increased pressure upon the institutions and the students.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On November 30 he said that he would consider proposing to the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. a ban on further Cruise missile deployment. Does the Minister's suggestion of November 30 mean that Canada will actively consider joining Belgium and other NATO advocates in calling for a moratorium on further Cruise missile deployment in Europe?

Mr. Speaker, as I have tried to make clear on two occasions in the House, we are considering whether, in light of the very encouraging initiative taken by the Soviet Union and the United States to resume discussions about nuclear arms control, there are initiatives or suggestions that it would be useful for Canada to make to both parties as a means of advancing that process. That is a matter which is still under very active consideration. I expect to be in a position to indicate whether we think it would be useful to take that kind of initiative, before the week is out. If we decide it would be useful to take initiatives of that kind, I will naturally indicate to the House the nature of any communication we would send to both parties in the context of trying to add to the success of the Geneva talks.
December 5, 1984

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister is not interested in joining Denmark, Greece, and other NATO partners in a nuclear freeze, and is not interested in joining the initiative which has now come from Belgium and other middle-sized NATO countries to call for a ban on deployment of Cruise missiles, how can we avoid the conclusion that he is not interested in any NATO initiatives except those that are authorized by the Pentagon?

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Why is it government policy at this time, in order to sweeten the deal about to be entered into between Canada and Turkey for the sale of some Buffalo STOL military aircraft, to add to it a gift

December 5, 1984

of some 20 CF-104 Starfighters, precisely when the NATO countries of Turkey and Greece are almost at the brink of going to war over the remilitarization of some of the islands in the eastern Aegean, especially when our own Canadian soldiers may be caught in the crossfire in Cyprus?

Is the Minister aware that yesterday in my constituency three persons escaped from the Bath Institution, possibly with outside help, then forcibly entered a home, terrorized two hostages, left them bound, and stole their car and three weapons? subtopic: MOTION TO ESTABLISH TASK FORCE ON REFORM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to wind up the remarks that I began several days ago on this topic. We were debating the establishment of the special committee to investigate the changes to the rules of the House of Commons. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, we had hit upon a rather unfortunate series of incidents. The various committees of the House were being struck under a set of rules and guidelines that ignored the long-standing traditions and past practices of those committees and of the House. It was a very difficult set of circumstances under which the changes to the rules of the House of Commons were to begin.
The Government had sent signals indicating that it was going to ignore a lot of the old traditions and past practices not only of this House but of parliamentary democracies all over the world. Members of our Party and Members of the Official Opposition as well expressed some doubts about opening up the process of reviewing the rules given the way we felt the
Parliamentary Reform
current Government had mishandled its very huge majority in committee.
With some trepidation we are now prepared to resume the study of the rules of the House of Commons even though we note, as I noted the other day, that such a committee had done substantive work in the previous Parliament and had made reports which had unanimous support, not all of which have been acted upon. I feel that it might have been in the interests of parliamentary reform if those reports had simply been acted upon rather than beginning a whole new round of parliamentary review.
We are hoping that the Government will keep its word to act in a responsible manner in spite of its very large majority. Now that the Government's mind has been jogged by events of the past few days, we hope that it will continue to recognize the need, if a parliamentary system is to operate properly, for the Opposition to have its firm rights and responsibilities guaranteed not only by the rules but by the precedents and traditions of the House. We hope that that will be the case and I am looking forward to hearing from the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn). I would hope that he would confirm that guarantee and read it into the record so that we can finalize the decision to set up such a committee.

Mr. Speaker, I want to add a few brief words to what,has already been said. As much as Members of the House are willing to entertain a proposal to have a special committee struck to change the rules of the House, I must say, and several of my colleagues are of the same opinion, that we question the Government's sincerity in doing this because at the same time as it was introducing such a motion, it was unilaterally changing the traditional rules under which we had operated. Specifically, Mr. Speaker, I draw your attention to the first meetings of the committees of this House.
A few weeks ago we attended the first meeting of the Agriculture Committee and several Members who are present today will recall what happened then. Just for your information, Mr. Speaker, what opposition members had to contend with on that particular day was a series of pre-printed resolutions introduced by government members in committee. I am told that these resolutions were unprecedented. One of these resolutions was introduced by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Blais) and was a resolution to have the committee sit in a mini-quorum fashion for the purposes of hearing witnesses, having only four government Members present and without a representative of the Opposition.
Needless to say, several members of the committee, particularly opposition members, were very upset by this proposal made on behalf of the Government. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) and I spoke extensively. As a matter of fact, the foundation meeting of the committee which traditionally lasts only a few minutes dragged on well into the better

December 5, 1984
Parliamentary Reform
part of an hour and a half on account of the very difficult situation in which the Government chose to place the Opposition.
As far as 1 and many of my colleagues are concerned, if Conservative members want to hear witnesses on their own, they can call such a meeting a Tory task force and not a parliamentary committee. If there are to be such Tory task forces, then Tory members can invite guests at the expense of the Tory Party and not at government expense. As well, they should publicly advertise that it is in fact a Tory task force that is sitting. On the other hand, if we are to have parliamentary committees, we should respect the traditions of Parliament which are that opposition members are to be present at such committees.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when there was a dispute in the House regarding how many Parties should be present in order to take a vote, the Government was made helpless for a number of days. A vote could not be taken when bells were being rung. The Government at that time simply had to wait for opposition members to return as per a ruling made by the Speaker. Everyone contended with that, as unfortunate as the incident was. Today, when the shoe is on the other foot, the Government says that it wants to be efficient. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture made a speech indicating that the Government should be efficient. Curtailing the role of opposition members was done in the name of efficiency.
Efficiency is a noble cause. We are all in favour of efficiency. I am sure that a dictatorship would be far less cumbersome than a democracy. However, we have not chosen to run our country by dictatorship. We have chosen to run it by parliamentary government and by responsible government through Members of the House of Commons. Having decided as a society to run our Government that way, I find the actions of the Government to be totally unreasonable.
This Government stated many times in the past during an election campaign which we can all remember that it was going to be open and accountable to Parliament. That was one of its 338 or so promises. It promised it would be respectful of Parliament's wishes. Government members said many other fine words to us during the election campaign.
Taking these actions in the name of efficiency is just not good enough. We in opposition are of the view that whenever a mini-quorum sits, there should be at least one opposition Member present. To refresh our memories, a minim-quorum means four Members sitting for the purposes of hearing a witness.
We are also of the view that the Member leading off in debate should always be a member of the Official Opposition according to the traditions of this House. Having myself come from another legislature, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that that is the way it was done there as well. The Official Opposition was usually recognized first in debate. I am sure that rule was not written down in any of the Standing Orders of that particular House of Assembly but it is an acknowledged principle under which Hon. Members always operated.
1 would hope that now that the Conservative Party has formed the Government of the country, it will afford as many courtesies to the Official Opposition as the previous Government afforded the Conservative Party when it was in opposition. If I can make one promise, it is that we will not abuse the rules the way Conservative members did.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his co-operation in allowing me to catch a plane.
I rise at this time to speak in favour of the motion of my colleague that the borrowing recommendations of this Government be changed. This is the first occasion, except for the period of Standing Order 21 statements and Question Period, on which I rise to speak in this House.
I would like to say a few words in relation to my election on September 4. The voters in my riding made two very important decisions on that day. First, like many other Canadians they decided enough was enough and that Liberals should no longer reign in this country. Where my constituents differed from a large majority of the population of Canada is that they saw through the promises made by the Conservative Party, realized that they were no different from the Liberals and opted instead for New Democratic representation in this House.
This Bill, Mr. Speaker, is yet one more example of why my constituents voted the way they did. If they had voted Conservative, they would have been voting for borrowing authority of $16 billion sight unseen, with no indication of what the money was going to be spent for. If I dared to vote in favour of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, my constituents would have every right to ask me to resign immediately. I want to thank those voters, Mr. Speaker, for their support and for their faith in my abilities. I also want to thank my riding association and the hundreds of persons who worked not only during the two-month pre-election period but who have worked over the last seven years to send me to this House. I would also like to take this opportunity to thank my family without whose support I would not be here.
I am very pleased to speak today on this Bill, Mr. Speaker, because this week marks a very important event in the riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan and in the neighbouring riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon. For the first time in a number of years citizens of those ridings who are cable subscribers are able to watch the House of Commons live without the aid of a converter. I noticed earlier today the former Member of Parliament for Thunder Bay-Atikokan was in the gallery, the now reincarnated commissioner for the CRTC. I am sure he will be pleased to know that whereas he was unable to make that change in the television service, I was successful.
The community of Thunder Bay and Atikokan and the parts in between have suffered much over the last number of years. This past winter there were over 14,000 people registered as out of work and looking for employment in our communities. That cost is staggering, Mr. Speaker. One of the reasons I am opposed to borrowing $16 billion without knowing what it is going to be spent on is that my constituents believe that they should know how this Government is going to deal with their unemployment situation. That unemployment problem is
December 5, 1984

extremely expensive. Unemployment insurance benefits last year for the Thunder Bay district amounted to $55.7 million. Welfare benefits for the City of Thunder Bay cost $2.5 million. Lost federal revenue over the same period amounted to $144 million. That is well over $200 million cost to the taxpayers of this land because of the unemployment situation in the Thunder Bay area, and it is the direct result, Mr. Speaker, of too many years of Liberal economic policies, which seem very clearly to be carrying through under the Conservative reign.
There is a plant in Thunder Bay called CanCar Rail Incorporated. It is a facility which was nationalized by Bill Davis and company, the Conservatives of Ontario. It is currently without functioning contracts. Its employees have been laid off for well over a year. In fact, in September ten employees became exhaustees of unemployment insurance; in October 150 employees became exhaustees; in November it was 100, and in December 25 to 50 employees have run out of unemployment insurance benefits. Those employees will not be getting back to work until June at the earliest. It is very clear that this new Government must act to provide some kind of income support in order to allow these people to survive over this long winter.
Before we approve any spending of this nature, we would also like to see what kind of urban transport policy will be put in place. What kind of program will there be for VIA to require the production of double-decker rail cars? Both of these things will have a big impact on the CanCar rail facilities.
Because the railroads and the Wheat Board could not come to an agreement last winter as to how much to pay to ship grain from Thunder Bay to the Seaway ports, over 1,000 men and women were laid off. This year it will be worse. The combination of poor crops in the lower Prairies and the two bridge failures we have experienced and are still experiencing will cause those lay-offs to occur again. In fact, there will be more people laid off and for a longer period of time.
We must do something about the capacity of the port of Thunder Bay. The lake shippers would like to have elevators which are almost full so that they can move their boats in and out very rapidly. The railways, on the other hand, would prefer to have the elevators nearly empty so they can move their cars in and out quickly. Thunder Bay is an extremely fine-tuned port. If nothing goes wrong on the rail or the water, everything moves smoothly. However, if there is a disaster on the rail lines which blocks CN or CP from coming in for any length of time, the port of Thunder Bay is in trouble. If the problem of the damaged bridge on the St. Lawrence had occurred in July, Mr. Speaker, the port of Thunder Bay would have shut down because it would have filled up very quickly.
The community of Atikokan was abandoned by the former Liberal government. It was only provided with make-work projects after the two mines closed. Every day in this House, Mr. Speaker, I am amazed at how we did not learn from the experience of Atikokan. We did not learn that we should not allow Canadian steel companies to purchase their iron ore from the United States. We did not learn that we should not
Borrowing Authority
allow companies to shut down communities arbitrarily, because it is not just mines we shut down, it is communities. Well, Atikokan is surviving, but no thanks to the federal Government. It is surviving due to individual initiative by the people in that community, but there are still some needs that have to be dealt with.
I noticed with interest that earlier this fall, when a mine closed in the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Government was very quick to provide some special assistance to that community. Well, the special assistance I need for the community of Atikokan is income support for those miners laid off in 1979 and 1980. Because of age and the damaged bodies they have as the result of many years in the mine, they need some kind of early retirement program which will allow them a decent level of survival. I want to know what kind of programs this Government will have next summer. 1 want to know now so I can tell the young people in my community what kind of jobs will be available to them. They are planning for their future and they want to make sure they can afford to go back to school next fall. So far this Government has done nothing but reduce the amount of employment opportunities.
There are many more things I could say about my community, but I will leave it at that for now. To summarize, I would just like to suggest that much has been said about the need to restore investor confidence in this country. What we really have been witnessing is nothing but a confidence game rather than a means of establishing confidence. We need a mechanism to ensure that people are put back to work. The majority of Canadians would prefer to work, whether it is in the home or outside. They would rather be doing that than collecting pogey or welfare. If we in the NDP were to support this Bill and the borrowing of $16 billion, we would be giving the Government a blank cheque and I do not think the people of Canada want us to do that.

Mr. Speaker, for me also this is the first opportunity I have to rise in this new Parlement, and I would like to take a few seconds to thank my constituents of Laurier for the confidence they showed me on September 4. I am very proud of the relationship I have established with so many people in my constituency from the time I was first elected in 1979, and I would like to give to all the men and women in my riding the assurance that I will do everything in my power to deserve their confidence during this new term of office.
I am very pleased to rise in this debate on borrowing authority, and I also note with great interest that the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) is here, listening to this debate, because I have a few comments on matters for which he is responsible.
I would first like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the statement made by the Minister of Linance (Mr. Wilson) and this bill
December 5, 1984

Borrowing Authority
requesting borrowing authority now before the House, coming so soon in the life of this new Parlement, prove to anyone who may still have any doubts about it the failure of this Progressive Conservative government. Perhaps you will say it is too early to make such an assessment, that I may be too critical. I do not think so, Mr. Speaker, and I will try to prove it within the next few minutes. Let us not forget that this Government was elected without a program and without goals. The only thing indeed that united that motley collection in the Progressive Conservative Party was that they were against the previous Liberal Government. Mr. Trudeau, the former Prime Minister, often reminded us that the Progressive Conservative Party represented all the people and all the elements in our society who were against something.

He referred on a number of occasions to that "coalition of antis".
[ Translation]
It sems rather obvious by now that there is no strategy and no plan. The only thing we can see is a sort of hardened position based on the Conservatives' blind faith that the deficit has to come down no matter what, and a few weeks ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) let the axe fall right and left without suggesting alternative solutions. They are now seeking our approval to borrow, but we do not have a budget, we do not have estimates.
The cutbacks ordered by the Conservative government are a fair indication of what it does not like, but we do not know what it likes. Our leader, the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) summed it up for us when he said: We will have to wait until spring to find out what this government likes. Mr. Speaker, that reminds me of a football team-I know you are a sports enthusiast and follow the game very closely-it reminds me of a football team whose defensive unit goes on the field, without a play-

The quarterback, as you know, Mr. Speaker, has to improvise. He goes into the huddle and scratches out the plays on the back of his hand or in the dirt. This is the kind of government we have today.
[ Translation]
The government of the Progressive Conservative Party has no plays, it is always in a huddle, and Canadians are left to hope that the huddle will not last too long. This blind obsession with cutting down the deficit will have a devastating impact in the field of science and technology, my responsibility as Opposition critic. The new government was hardly sworn in that it rushed to cut research tax credits. A few weeks later, we heard the statement of the Minister of Finance and whole programs of energy and environmental research were terminated, whole programs of summer employment for youths and students, Summer Canada, labour training programs were cancelled, and all that in spite of the challenging promises of
this government which was supposed to promote research in this country.

1 remember that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was Leader of the Opposition last March or April, he made a speech and said that we must double research and development spending in this country and triple our resolve to reach it.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
But what have we seen? We have seen the contrary.
I am very pleased to see the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) here today. Earlier today I spoke to the chairman of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and asked him if we could conduct hearings into the cutting, the slicing, the destruction of the energy division at the National Research Council. The Minister is very well aware of that. I cannot believe that this is what this Government intended. Something went wrong some place. I just cannot believe that it has embarked upon such a foolhardy path.
1 would like to read into the record a letter to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), a copy of which was sent to the Minister of State for Science and Technology. It is from the Faculty of Engineering at the University of Waterloo. The author states:
*	(1550)
The curtailment of the 61-man Division of Energy at the National Research Council is a great blow to Research and Development in renewable energy. What the government has done has far reaching negative consequences, specifically:
*	Loss of jobs in the private sector, estimated at around 1500 to 2000. These are mainly in the small business sector.
*	Loss of export potential for made-in-Canada renewable energy and energy conservation products.
*	Loss of inflow of technical know-how through loss of participation in the International Energy Agency activities.
*	Loss of highly skilled personnel at NRC and elsewhere whose efforts have put Canada in the forefront of alternative energy research.
In a similar letter from the Brace Research Institute Faculty of Engineering at Macdonald College of McGill University, the authors summarize some letters they have written to the Minister of State for Science and Technology and to the head of the solar energy program at the National Research Council. They write:
We feel that the Conservative Government is adopting a policy to completely dismantle the entire Canadian renewable energy industry which has a great potential for providing employment and small business opportunities for Canadians.
They are undertaking this dismantling operation without any consultation-
This puts the lie to every single promise that that Government and its Leader made.
-of those of us in the private sector who freely gave of our time and efforts to establish with the previous regimes, programmes destined to stimulate the Canadian economy.
They are ignoring the fact that Canada will host a World Forum of Renewable Energy in June 1985.
December 5, 1984

They are not diversifying our R&D capabilities in energy. Instead of undertaking R&D to create jobs they are putting us at the mercy of foreign imports.
I have several other letters which I will not be able to get to today, Mr. Speaker. I will conclude by saying that the Government has again provided us with no alternative. It has told us what it does not like. Presumably it does not like the energy division of the National Research Council. It does not like the summer employment program for students. They have not told us how these cuts are going to stimulate investment in the private sector.
I wish the Conservatives would explain to us how Canadian businesses are going to be taking more risks and how they are going to be putting up the research and development monies which we need in the country. The only answer they have is that these cuts will somehow reduce the deficit. Presumably they might lead to lower interest rates which would lead to further investments, except that in his statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) states very clearly that interest rates in Canada depend upon the United States.

Last Friday, November 30, less than three months after the election of this new government, was a historic day in Canada. For the first time, I heard one reporter-there might have been others-suggest that this government would only last one term.

In his column Don McGillivray stated:
The Tories don't look invincible now. It's strange now to remember the forecasts of only a couple of months ago that they would be unbeatable for a generation.
After the goofs of recent days, it's possible to see this as a one-term government, disintegrating like the government of John Diefenbaker did.
I rest my case, Mr. Speaker. I think I have read into the record ample evidence to demonstrate the intellectual bankruptcy of the Government. It will not take long before the Government starts to plummet rapidly in the polls of the country and in the confidence of the voters of Canada.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the legislation which is currently before the House, namely Bill C-ll, the borrowing authority Bill. The Conservative Government is seeking authority to borrow $7.3 billion in the present fiscal year, 1984-85, plus $16 billion for the fiscal year 1985-86 for which it has not tabled, or does it intend to table, estimates until next spring. In essence, the Conservatives are asking us to accept, de facto, that they will seek to spend the people's money in the best interests of the people.
I suggest that the best interests of the largest percentage of the population are not being considered at all. In fact, the beautiful rhetorical phrases that the Government has used, is using and plans to continue using cover a travesty of its actions and its lack of concern for the majority of the population. They feel that they can lull us all into insensitivity to the real issues and the real plight by talking about, for example, imposing a minimum tax on the rich, which essentially will be a small amount of money in the total picture and certainly will not assure that justice and equity will be achieved. They think it will and plan to go merrily along their way implementing these unconscionable cuts which will surely severely affect the majority. We shall not be duped.
In its November 8 economic statement the federal Government announced that it planned to reduce its spending in the fiscal year by $4.2 billion through program expenditure reductions, eliminations and increased cost recovery. Of these reductions some $515 million, or 12 per cent of the total, can be said to be social-type expenditures. For example, expenditures of the Department of Employment and Immigration would be reduced by $432.3 million in 1984-85. Among the programs affected by the cuts will be the Mobility Program, the General Industrial Training Program, Young Workers Exchange Program and the Summer Canada Program. It is also anticipated that this Department's expenditures will be reduced by $200 million by tightening interviewing procedures to ensure that only those who are entitled receive benefits. I think, Mr. Speaker, you will recognize Flora's private snoopers there. I think that is a disgrace.
Another $90 million is expected to be saved by considering severance pay and pension income as earnings when determining the eligibility for unemployment insurance. Thus, workers who lose their jobs would not receive unemployment insurance benefits until they exhaust their company pension and their severance pay. This is a mean and reactionary cut-back that

December 5, 1984
Borrowing Authority
affects the least protected in our society and I believe has created much discontent.
Cut-backs in employment programs can be particularly consequential for women, young people, the handicapped and visible minorities. 1 suggest that these groups constitute a majority of our population. These groups suffer from higher than average unemployment rates and need special assistance to find work. The unemployment rate for women between the ages of 35 and 44 who return to work when their children enter school is much higher than that for men.
With the increasing need for two incomes in the family and with the increase in self-supporting women as a result of separation, divorce or their being unmarried mothers, the number of women looking for work is much greater than it was a few years ago.
With the workplace in transition, the need for training and retraining programs becomes an imperative for our new entrants to the workplace and those displaced by new technology. Since they do not have access to adequate training programs, the cut of $40 million in the General Industrial Training Program hits very hard. Women account for approximately 23 per cent of the trainees in this program. There must be an ongoing response to those who have difficulty finding work. The Government does not seem to be looking hard for those solutions.
The highest unemployment rate is among young people with very little or no previous work experience. That unemployment rate is close to 18 per cent. Although staying in school longer is one of the employment solutions, Canada student loans have been cut back by $5 million and $3 million has been cut from the Young Workers Exchange program and $85 million has been cut from Summer Canada. Without student loans and assistance in finding summer jobs, many young people will be forced to quit school. Yet many cannot find work. It is a vicious circle. The promises of action some time in the spring do not answer their need to develop to their fullest potential.
I believe the Government is completely forgetting about the finest natural resource that we have, our human resource. It has forgotten how one should go about developing that resource. Let me bring to the attention of the House an article that appeared in Le Droit today-

-where it is stated: "Champagne avoids the real problems."
The Minister Mrs. Champagne, who is also responsible for the coordination of activities related to the International Year for Youth in 1985, performed an incredible feat when she did not mention once in her speech the unemployment problem affecting 17 per cent of our young people between 15 and 24 years of age.
She did not refer either to the programs planned by her government. The young people were clearly disappointed when the Minister representing them in the government did not say a word or make a single policy statement about their future. I find that absolutely shocking, Mr. Speaker.

Another important area that I would like to bring to the attention of the House is the expenditure cuts in housing. A cut of $9.6 million will affect social housing expenditures whose object is to assist Canadians whose income is insufficient to gain access to adequate housing. Another $29.4 million will be cut from the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, the object of which is the repair and modernization of existing houses and the improvement of housing and living conditions. In my riding of Mount Royal there is a tremendous number of old stock housing which is in serious disrepair and badly in need of renovation. We also have a high demand for co-op housing. These are the exact areas which the Government has chosen to cut.
My constituents and other Canadians with whom I have talked are obviously not saying the same things that the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) or the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) have heard. That is of great concern to me. We must either speak louder or improve their hearing aids.
With respect to social housing, there are only 147 transition houses which provide emergency shelter, safe houses and second stage housing. We need many more. Only 45 per cent of Canada's population lives in an area with a shelter for battered women and most workers feel that funds need to be increased before real inroads can be made in attempting to address the housing shortage for battered women. In the last 20 years there has been an acute increase of single parent families from 6.5 per cent to 10.4 per cent. Elderly women are in serious need of protected housing. The Government's commitment to Canadians in need has reflected itself in decreased grants. These cut-backs seriously jeopardize the health and welfare of the general public.
In conclusion, the extent of the cut-backs may affect the service-producing industries in which women, youth, the handicapped and visible minorities are involved. I cannot support the budget or this Bill until we have some idea of what the Government plans to do.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have learned one thing in the years that I have been here, most of which have been during Liberal governments. This Bill has amply and vividly demonstrated that message. I have learned that the more things change, the more they are the same.
We are being asked to give the Government authority to borrow more money to finance its expenditures until the end of this fiscal year in March, 1985. That is a standard procedure which we see almost every year and to which we have no objection. However, the other aspect of the Bill is a proposal to allow the Government to borrow $16 billion for the next fiscal year.
The reason I began my remarks by saying that the more things change the more they are the same is that the Liberal government introduced a similar Bill. No one fought such a Bill more strenuously than the Official Opposition at the time,
December 5, 1984

which is now the Government. When we dealt with a similar Bill in 1982, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), who was then the Leader of the Official Opposition, moved a motion. In that motion he said that the granting of authority for the borrowing of a sum greater than the amount which is required to meet the Government's need to the end of the current fiscal year is objectionable in principle and that the House therefore declines to give second reading. What the Secretary of State for External Affairs was objecting to then is precisely what his Government is asking the House to approve at this time.
While we are not opposed to the Government borrowing funds to meet its expenditures, we are opposed to giving the Government a blank cheque for the next year, for the same reasons which the Conservatives gave when they were in opposition. We have no budget for the coming year. We have no details or explanation of the kind of programs the Government proposes to put into effect. We certainly have no explanation in any detail about what cuts in existing programs it proposes to make. When we see the cuts that the Government has already made in this year's programs, we can have nothing but fear about what it proposes to do.
This is not the only government that has a deficit. I point out to Members of the House that every government in Canada, including the previous Liberal government, the present federal Government and every provincial government, including Conservative, NDP, Social Credit and Parti Quebe-cois governments, have deficits. Even if there was a Liberal provincial government, it would have a deficit. Every provincial government has a deficit, not because they are overspending but because of the slowdown in the economy, the recession. Revenues are down. They are substantially lower than those governments had calculated. The only way in which they could operate without deficits would be by having major cut-backs in the services which provincial governments provide for the people in their provinces, and the people are not ready to accept that.
We do not have deficits because we are overspending. We have deficits because revenues are not what they should be. If our economy was working as it should be and instead of 11.5 per cent unemployment we had a 5, 6 or 7 per cent rate of unemployment, deficits would be very small.
Ten of the most prominent economists in academic communities in Ontario and Quebec and in think-tanks such as the C. D. Howe Institute have agreed that the Government should try to reduce the deficit. They have said that along with proposals to reduce the deficit, the Government needs to get the Bank of Canada to ease its monetary and fiscal policies. We cannot do much as long as we have interest rates such as those which prevail today.
We are told that interest rates are down substantially from what they were. However, the real interest rate-that is, the difference between the increase in the cost of living and the interest rates charged-is not down very much from the time
Borrowing Authority
when it was 20 per cent. It is now down by eight points, but the rate of inflation has also been reduced by the same amount. The real interest rate is very high and it will continue to be high as long as the Conservative Government follows the same advice which the former Liberal government received and permits the Governor of the Bank of Canada to tie our interest rate policy to the American interest rate rather than to have a policy which meets the needs of Canadians.
I oppose this Bill not only because it gives the Government money for the next fiscal year, but because I am very apprehensive about the kinds of cuts the Government has made in its desire, intention and determination to reduce the deficit. First of all, the Government cut back on programs which helped people in greatest need. I should like to give a few illustrations. It has cut back on housing programs which are very important to older people and people in the lower income brackets. It has cut CHIP by $84 million. There are thousands of homes in every city in Canada which were built 60 to 100 years ago. Those homes are energy inefficient. This program helped to rehabilitate such homes and help people save hundreds of dollars per year in heating costs. It was not only important to the individuals in those homes who benefited from the program; it helped cut down on the amount of heating oil and non-renewable energy resources which were being depleted at a rapid rate.
The Government has also cut $29.4 million from RRAP. In every city there are older homes which are falling into a state where they are virtually unusable. As a result of this program, funded in part by the federal Government and in part by provincial governments, tens of thousands of older homes in poor areas of our cities have been modernized and rehabilitated, have been rewired and replumbed. For the Government to cut back on that kind of program is a disgrace. Similarly there have been cuts in the funding of public housing. If there is one area in which the governments of Canada, federal and provincial, ought to be ashamed of themselves, it is in their programs to provide adequate housing for people in lower income brackets. I am thinking of people on welfare and single parent families. Their incomes are too low for them to obtain adequate housing. They need rental rates which they can afford, yet that is the kind of program which the Government cuts back by $9.5 million.
There are thousands of young people attending university. The only way in which they can continue to attend university is by finding work in the summer, yet the Government cut Summer Canada programs by $85 million.
I could continue but I see Mr. Speaker indicating that my time is up. In conclusion, the cuts in the budget which the Government has made are the worst ones it could have made, even if I agreed that cuts were required, and I do not.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak to Bill C-ll. I do not think anyone will be surprised to hear that I disagree with the Bill as presented by the Government. One reason is that I do not think we can really trust a Government and a Party that asks the House for borrowing authority for next year, without bringing down a new budget, without tabling the Estimates. Why we should not trust this Government? Well, what this Government has achieved, or rather has failed to achieve since the election campaign and its outcome on September 4, shows why it cannot be trusted.
For instance, the Government promised it would create jobs, but if we look at the mini-budget, all it contains are cutbacks and potential lay-offs and unemployment. I see the Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) opposite. This Government made a commitment to engage in consultation and to refrain from unilateral decisions. The first thing the new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs did was to ignore the people who take care of UFFI cases, and instead made a unilateral decision, that is, he recommended to Treasury Board that cuts be made in the program.
Another example is subsidized housing. During the election campaign, Members in all ridings promised co-operative housing when they were in the Opposition, and they were asking for more funds. But lo and behold: the mini-budget provides for cuts in subsidized housing and the RRAP program.
Mr. Speaker, I can think of another area as well where the Prime Minister said 'with his hand on his heart' that he would never tamper with the universality of our programs. And what do we see now? A document that challenges the universality of those same programs. Not only Liberal Members, not only New Democratic Party Members are saying that we can no longer trust this Government. I know some Members of the Progressive Conservative Party, senior Members, who are starting to feel uncomfortable. They did not expect their Government to act this way. As for the junior Members, sooner or later they will wake up as well. After Christmas they also will start to react. There are also the media, and I would like to quote from an article by Lysianne Gagnon in the newspaper La Presse, in which she comments on the universality issue, and I quote:
"With his hand on his heart-"
August 1984: on every platform, with his hand on his heart and in solemn tones, Brian Mulroney repeated that he would never never challenge the principle of universality for social programs: that is, he said, "a sacred trust".
August 1984: in the riding of Saint-Hyacinthe, Andree Champagne, the Progressive Conservative candidate, is indignant. Her Liberal opponent had the effrontery to distribute in the riding a speech by John Crosbie in which he said it would be necessary to revise the universality of social programs and keep them for the people who really need them. At a press conference, Mrs. Champagne protested that it was "monstrous" to scare senior citizens with the "purely personal" thoughts of Mr. Crosbie. (One would have to suppose that Mrs. Champagne was oblivious to the fact that Mr. Crosbie was not exactly an unknown within the Party, being the former Minister of Finance and the Opposition critic for finance. Less discreet than his colleagues, he had shown the
Party's true colours at the beginning of the election campaign, when he was soundly reprimanded by his leader.)
November 1984: the Mulroney Government announced its intention to review the universality of social programs.
For the time being, only old age pensions and family allowance would be on the review list, so they said. The Prime Minister, his hand on his heart and with sincerity in his voice, swore that he would never tamper with medicare.
One wonders whether that is not precisely the government's ultimate goal.
Why this nagging doubt? And why not? When one has been lied to once with so many solemn promises, the odds are that it could happen again. But there are other indications.
Anyone who believes that the Government's main objective in challenging the universality principle is to give more to the poor is naive beyond belief. This is a good selling point, but in fact, everything suggests that this is not a transfer of funds to assist the disadvantaged, but simply an initiative to save the government some money, in line with the main obsession of the Mulroney Government which is to reduce the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, I think that more and more, in all walks of life, virtually the only people left who have any confidence in this Government are the Conservative Members of Parliament, and that is why we cannot grant this Government the requested borrowing power because of its lack of credibility.
Today and last Friday, I asked a question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about spouse allowances for people between the ages of 60 and 64. In reply to my questions, the Prime Minister himself said that he was willing to help all needy people between 60 and 64, but in fact, the government is only helping the small group of widows and widowers between 60 and 64. This discrimates against those between the ages of 60 and 64 who have the same needs and the same income, but who are single, separated or divorced.
Mr. Speaker, we know that the initiative announced by the Minister will provide assistance to 85,000 people at a cost of S300 million. However, what the Prime Minister and the Minister did not tell us, and what the Conservative Members certainly do not know, is that the Governments will save about SI70 million of these $300 million because about 40 percent of those who will become eligible for the new program were already eligible for welfare benefits, which means that the Government is giving with one hand and taking away with the other. Instead of helping a greater number of people, the Government is now depriving 340,000 people aged between 60 and 64 who live alone, of the right to spouse allowance or old age security pension with guaranteed income supplement.
Mr. Speaker, I do not trust the Prime Minister, but 1 do trust the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), as he and perhaps the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) are the only members of Cabinet to defend the rights of ordinary Canadians. What about the rest of them? We know where they come from. They are more interested in defending the multinationals. I trust that, with the assistance of some of the Members opposite who will very
December 5, 1984

soon be receiving visits from senior citizens, these other members of Cabinet can also be made more aware of the situation.
I am confident that this will happen because I know some of the Conservative Members, and they are honest people who will defend these senior citizens in the interest of all Canadians. I do not believe this cause to be partisan, either Liberal, NDP, Conservative; rather, all Members of this House and all Canadians should make it their cause to guarantee that the legislation passed by this Government will be fair and will really meet the needs of people between 60 and 64 who live alone. And we know that the very great majority are women, and I am confident that when the legislation is introduced the Government will have mended its ways, and instead of discriminating against a group of people for reasons of marital status, they will introduce a bill that will meet the needs of the entire population.
There is another important issue the Government will give us a chance to discuss and that is the universality of social programs. I have already suggested how sad it was for the Government's approach to foster class struggle. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister himself has made a comparison-is it normal that someone earning $500,000 should get family allowances? And the documents tabled by the Minister of Finance reflected the class struggle existing between those earning from $20,000 to $30,000, from $40,000 to $50,000.
In my view, there are enough devisive factors in Canada as you are very much aware Mr. Speaker, that we should not be creating new ones. Speaking on the issue of universality, we need only look at the tables provided by the Government-if there is an area where the rich are favoured, it is not through program universality but through tax exemptions.
Let us consider the support which the Government provides for families with children, that is the family allowances. A taxpayer earning less than $10,000 gets $359, while another taxpayer earning $80,000 is left with $175 per year after tax. Let us turn now to the child exemptions based on the income tax tables. People earning less than $10,000 pay no income tax at all. They have zero income. People earning $80,000 get a $363 tax saving.

Mr. Speaker, this is an outrageous piece of legislation before us today in Bill C-ll. It is the sort of thing the Conservatives opposed in opposition, the sort of thing they said ought never to happen. They were very critical of borrowing for expenditures that had not been specified in a Budget. They were very critical when the Liberals did this. In terms of contempt for the public and disregard for Parliament, the Conservatives are indeed the equal of the Liberal Party.
We have before us today a proposal that $23.3 billion be borrowed. Of this amount, $16 billion is for expenditures for
Borrowing Authority
the following fiscal year. We do not have any details of that. Of the $7.3 billion for expenditures for the remainder of the fiscal year, $2 billion is for a very loosely defined contingency fund; in other wrods, an expenditure which is totally inappropriate.
We are not opposed to borrowing in principle. Obviously every government has to borrow. If we were in government, we would have to borrow as well. It is what the borrowing is for, specifically the justification for the program. We either have no detail or we have the proposals in the economic statement, in effect a short-term mini-budget which shows that the Government's expenditures are short-sighted and misguided.
An alternative to borrowing more is to raise the money by taxes, specifically by closing the loopholes by which many people avoid paying taxes. This could be the source of an enormous amount of money. This Government does not choose to pursue that option which is open to it. It would be more fair for the Canadian public when medium and low income earners are having to pay very high taxes because corporations and better off individuals are benefiting from these enormous loopholes. The economic proposals that we have in the economic statement show that the Government is making important cuts in some areas. I think these cuts could be characterized as being harmful enough in certain areas to hurt the agencies concerned.
I can think of cuts to expenditures in the area of arts and culture. We are seeing cuts which total under $100 million. That is really not enough money to help the deficit. However, that amount of money is very important to an area like arts and culture in which expenditures have not been generous. Cuts to this area mean that particular companies cannot perform, programs will have to be cut back, artists and writers will not get grants, books and magazines will not be published, and all kinds of activities which are important to the cultural life of Canada will not happen. This cut-back particularly affects artists who, on average, are low-income earners. Spectacular monetary successes in the artistic world are few and far between. The average performing artist or writer lives on a very modest income and a very high proportion of them actually live below the poverty line.
There have been no cost-of-living or general increases to funding in the area of arts and culture over the last decade. Now its funding is getting cut and those cuts are sufficient to hurt arts and culture. However, what is $100 million when we have a deficit as large as we do? If we really want to attack the deficit, we must take much sterner measures and go after the lost revenue. We would go after tax loopholes and tax expenditures for corporations if we were really serious about the deficit.
Let me turn to some of the specific cuts contained in the economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). There was a cut to the Summer Canada Program, a program which employed students in the summer. This program certainly provided excellent projects for the riding of Broadview-

December 5, 1984

Greenwood. It provided good jobs for students and helped local agencies and people. The program gave young people a good opportunity to work.
Cuts have been made to the Canada Oil Substitution Program. Goodness knows we need to be working on oil substitution and better conservation measures for this important nonrenewable resource. However, cuts have been made to that program.
Cuts have been made to the CHIP program and there have been reductions in funding to energy research and development. There have been really misguided cuts in the budget affecting science and technology. There have been cuts to radiation research, pollution research, research on the extent of damage caused by the spruce budworm, Canada wildlife research and a toxicology centre which has been doing very important research. These were important programs. However, the amount of money gained by these cuts is not significant in terms of reducing the budget deficit. This harm is being caused by shortsighted policies and is not a serious attack on the deficit which the Government says it is really trying to attack.
Cuts have been made to the 1986 census. There has been a 25 per cent reduction to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, something which will affect a lot of people. There was a cut of $180 million to external aid. Yet the Government talks about increases in its aid to Ethiopa. I remind the House that among these cuts to external aid are cuts to IDRC, to CIDA and to projects in which Ethiopa took part. On the one hand there is the pretence of being more generous by meeting a crisis, and on the other hand there are cut-backs in perhaps less glamorous programs but ones which are very important to attacking the problem of under-production of food and under-development. Surely it is that kind of aid with which we must be equally concerned.
A cut of $9.6 million has been made to the CMHC social housing program. Co-ops and public housing will be hit. Co-ops need more money, not less. We in Canada have a very good co-op system. There are many people who are on waiting lists for co-ops. There are plans for co-ops to be built. It is an excellent form of housing. There is a crying need for public housing. There are homeless people, families doubled up and families living in inadequate housing because the private market is building housing which is not affordable for a great many individuals and families. Yet there are budget cuts to this very critical area.
I suggest that the Government might do better by looking for its economic ideas in the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada. Just last week, the Economic Council of Canada published its annual review and recommended that there not be budget cuts of the nature of those made. The Council suggested that the Government ought instead to increase its revenues. The Council does take the deficit problem seriously. It thought there should be a conservative attack on the deficit but it did recommend the following:
Our research .. . shows that much of the fiscal plight of governments today is of their own making, since they have forgone in various ways revenues that in earlier days they were able to levy effectively.
Of course, the Council is speaking of the taxing of wealthier individuals and particularly of corporations, a sector which is paying less and less of the tax burden. The Economic Council of Canada notes that corporate income taxes provide only 10 per cent of the revenue of the Government of Canada, while personal income taxes provide up to 28 per cent of it. Corporations at one time paid a lot more than that.
The Economic Council of Canada very cautiously recommends that tax increases be implemented by the elimination of exemptions and loopholes and by the imposition of very modest rate increases. This is an alternative that could be considered instead of these vicious cuts to social and public housing, co-ops and external aid.
There are a great many tax loopholes and exemptions available. Taxes forgone through RRSPs, for example, amount to $2.6 billion. That is an enormous amount of money. Yet the cuts to arts and culture expenditures amount to under $100 million. That shows that the Government does not have the right priorities. It is tampering with important and vital programs but is not going after moneys that are available to it. These moneys could be tapped into, retaining more money for the vital social programs of Canada. Fast resource write-offs-
