Mr. Speaker, 1 was not prepared, I did not expect to speak today, but while listening to the Hon. Members opposite, I told myself: What nonsense! I must rise in this debate. As you know, memory is the faculty that forgets. Hon. Members opposite do not seem to recall that not so long ago, they were governing this country and the pandora's box which was inherited from them and which we have had to open, was not as interesting as we had hoped at first.
Therefore, this borrowing authority is requested to clean up the mess left by the previous administration. We have to make a review in order to borrow that money.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, some Hon. Members opposite do not seem to-For instance, I feel that my colleague the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) is too easily influenced by the old guard of her party who have certainly failed to tell her how their government was run. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, you certainly remember something which adversely affected my riding, namely, the wanton expropriation at Mirabel by the Canada Lands Company. That is the perfect example of mismanagement. Do you realize that they found it necessary to expropriate a surplus of 80,000 acres of land for an airport for which only 17,000 acres were required-As you know, this was paid for with public funds and today it is things like those-
December 5, 1984

An Eton. Member from Western Canada was telling me today that in Alberta there are facilities which were leased by the previous government and which are now costing millions of dollars, although they are not being used-All these things we must cope with now.
I do not intend to start a long debate on this, but I feel 1 must provide the House with some examples which I think are significant. My hon. friend referred to our senior citizens. I cannot agree that the programs and services which are necessary for the maintenance and growth of the primary industries on Prince Edward Island should be subjected to such radical cut-backs.
Let us examine agriculture. The dairy research program will be eliminated and special export payments for dairy products will be restricted. What effect will this have on dairy exports? What effect will it have, for example, on the sale of evaporated milk from Prince Edward Island to the Algerian market? What effect will it have on the sale of cheese from Prince Edward Island to foreign markets? Those are serious considerations that arise out of the economic statement.
The federal Department of Agriculture will be reducing its operating expenditures and restricting grants and contributions in such areas as livestock improvement. If we talked to most small farmers and farmers in Prince Edward Island in general, we would find that it was a very good program. Canagrex was eliminated before it had a chance to prove its worth. That was a very important program. I realize there was some opposition to it, but, in general, Prince Edward Islanders were for Canagrex. Farm organizations have already criticized the elimination of Canagrex.
Additional levies will be imposed by the federal Government for services such as food inspection. We should think about that. In Prince Edward Island 80 per cent of the potatoes produced go on the export market. To reduce inspection could be devastating. The Island is basically disease-free but has diseases such as ring rot. If that disease got on the foreign markets, Prince Edward Island would lose those markets. It would be the end of the potato industry in Prince Edward Island, or wherever potatoes are grown in Canada.
The agricultural input quality assurance and records of livestock performance will be eliminated. What effect will that have on Island farmers? Those are matters which should concern each and every Member of Parliament; not just opposition Members, but also government members.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill we are debating now is a classic example of the kind of political move which breeds cynicism about politics and political parties. It brings into question the credibility of the Official Opposition of just a few years ago. What is the Canadian public to think-those who pay attention to these matters- about a Progressive Conservative Government which now requests Parliament to do the very same thing that those Hon. Members, when they were in opposition, so self-righteously and indignantly condemned. This is the sort of thing which breeds cynicism. One has to ask just what the Official Opposition of just a few years ago had in mind. The only conclusion one can come to is that at that time they were insincere in their protests. We remember all the rhetoric about the abuse which was being heaped on Parliament by the Liberal Government. We heard then that in coming to Parliament and asking for this kind of borrowing authority the Liberals obviously had no respect for the long tradition of parliamentary scrutiny of parliamentary expenditures, and it was this situation, in part, which helped the Conservatives to get the mandate they did. People had a sense, and rightfully so, that the Liberals were abusing Parliament. Now we have a Conservative Government
and instead of an indication that this Government does indeed want to depart from the attitude towards Parliament which it so righteously condemned just a short while ago, we get identical action. There must be bewilderment on the part of a great many Canadians who voted Conservative on the basis that they considered the Liberals were disrespectful of Parliament and who thought some change might be forthcoming.
I feel it is particularly ironic, Mr. Speaker, that we should be debating Bill C-ll on the same day that a motion was finally passed to bring in to being a special task force on parliamentary reform. The objections of the Official Opposition to this kind of Bill just a few years ago were based on its understanding and respect for Parliament. And on the very day we begin what I hope will be a genuine process of parliamentary reform, we see before us in Bill C-ll an unfortunate indication that the new Government is no more respectful of Parliament, and no more willing to change, at least at this point, than the previous Government. Therefore, I say, Mr. Speaker, as one who will be part of that new task force on parliamentary reform, that I intend to go into it with the kind of positive and hopeful attitude which I know is absolutely necessary if that committee is to finally have an effect on the life of this Parliament and on the House of Commons for years to come. I am disappointed at the same time, Mr. Speaker, and I am taking this opportunity to say so-because I unfortunately did not participate in the debate surrounding the creation of the task force itself-that the new Government did not seize the opportunity to show good faith when it came to the issue of parliamentary reform. It did not use the mandate it received from the Canadian public, partly as a result of its rightful criticism of the Liberals and their attitude towards Parliament, to begin by making a few changes. The committee will have to spend many hours trying to arrive at what it hopes will be the right recommendations so that Government will finally act. It would have been a spur to that committee to have received any sign whatsoever that the Government actually was open to change. It also would have been a sign of hope, not just to members of that task force, but to all Hon. Members of Parliament, and to everyone concerned about parliamentary reform. We did not receive that indication, Mr. Speaker. Instead we got a hassle with respect to quorums in committee and who had to be present when we were to hear evidence.
The Government could have taken the opportunity to adopt some of the unanimous all-party recommendations by the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure of the last Parliament. The recommendation which comes most quickly to mind is with respect to the election of the Speaker. Purely from a tactical point of view, Mr. Speaker, the Government could have determined who it wanted to be Speaker. I say this with no reflection on who actually became Speaker because I happen to believe the present Speaker is doing an excellent job. However, the Government could have seized the opportunity to adopt the recommendations of the Special Committee with respect to the process by which we elect the
December 5, 1984

Speaker. It would have been assured of having its own way, in any event, given the massive majority it has in the House.
Government could have given the House of Commons more control over its own life by bringing in changes with respect to the Commissioners of Internal Economy, by having all-party representation either on that committee or by changing the various structures by which the House administers itself. There were a number of recommendations with which the Government could have proceeded, but it did not. I, for one, am disappointed. Nevertheless, I will go into the work of the new task force on parliamentary reform with a positive and hopeful attitude, knowing that the chairman is serious about parliamentary reform. I am sure that all Hon. Members who have been assigned to that particular task force by their respective parties are also serious about parliamentary reform.
I would like to comment, in the context of the borrowing authority, on the over-all strategy of the Government. I, as the environment critic for the New Democratic Party, have been particularly concerned about the cut-backs in Environment Canada. I am very concerned about the reductions in federal Government programs in the Canadian Wildlife Service of the Department of the Environment. I would just like to take what time I have left to say that the cut-backs in the Canadian Wildlife Service with respect to wildlife toxicology projects, projects to rehabilitate endangered species, conservation of international wildlife, and wildlife interpretation, are, in my view, a classic example of short-sightedness. It is a classic example of being pennywise and pound foolish. It is a tragic failure on the part of this Government because any real long-term, stable economic growth will have to be based on an economic model which does not put environmental concerns aside for the moment in order to have economic growth, thus setting up a false dichotomy between healthy economic growth and environmental matters. The Government should see that at some point we will have to develop a way of thinking economically that faces up to the fact that long-term, stable economic growth has to take environmental considerations into account. What we have here on the part of the Government is not that realization. In fact it is, as I say, a tragic failure to make that connection.
I can only hope that over the course of the next weeks, months or years, however long it takes, by working with others concerned about the Canadian environment, indeed the global environment, we can bring this Government to realize that this is indeed short-sighted and it should begin to see the world differently.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be taking part in this debate, because it is a very important one. I want to say a few words in the other official language. The question at issue in this debate is: what is the Government going to do with the money for which it is seeking borrowing authority from the House? The Govern-
Borrowing Authority
ment has given us no information on how the borrowed funds are going to be used. That is a very important matter, Mr. Speaker.
Second, I want to ask this Government how it can justify borrowing large sums of money without providing information. Is this how the Government respects Parliament?
Third, I want to ask the Government how it can possibly ask for permission to borrow a lot of money while at the same time wanting to give the public the impression that it is eager to reduce the deficit.

This is an important debate on three important questions, Mr. Speaker. What is the purpose of the spending for which authorization is sought to borrow this money here today? What is the Government's attitude toward the notion of accountability of the executive to Parliament? How can the Government, without any credibility whatsoever, come before us to borrow large sums of money at the same time that it preaches frugality to the public?
Dealing with the first question, the Government is asking to borrow $23.3 billion, $7 billion for this fiscal year, of which $2 billion is for a discretionary fund. The Government has not identified the purpose for which that money will be spent. It just wants to have the money on hand without specifically identifying what it is for. Could the Government possibly be borrowing this $23.3 billion for a worth-while public purpose? If so, it would be incumbent upon us to give the request serious consideration. Since the Government has not provided us with information regarding the $16 billion for the next fiscal year or the $2 billion in the discretionary fund for this fiscal year, we are left to wonder and speculate about what it wants to spend the money on. Therefore, I would like to posit some possible and useful public purposes for which the Government could use this money, which would then make it incumbent upon us to consider the request seriously.
For example, if it were seeking the money to invest so that the public would get a decent return, we would know it was going to be put to a useful purpose and would not be wasted. However, the Government has given us no information. In fact, it has deferred needed public works for both this fiscal year and next. Public works not only put people back to work but also provide facilities to serve communities for many years to come. It is bad enough that the Government cancelled public works, but even worse than that, it has deferred them. By doing that, the Government is admitting that those public works will have to be done in the future. Obviously they will have to be done at a higher cost than the cost at which they could be done today, and they will be done at a time when inflation is higher than it is today, so it will cost more to do them. That is a waste of public money.
If these people across the way, Mr. Speaker, were to borrow for a useful purpose, we could consider the request very seriously. But their actions have demonstrated that they are not seeking to borrow for a useful purpose. The Government could be borrowing for the useful purpose of better insulating

December 5, 1984
Borrowing Authority
homes so that energy could be better conserved. This could be done if we were to make dollars available to home owners so that they could insulate their homes properly. That would be a useful public investment. Electrical utilities in the United States have found that it is cheaper to produce electricity through conservation than it is through the construction of new hydro facilities, for example. Investment in conservation gives a real return. If this Government were to say that it wants to borrow money to provide for better insulation in homes across this country, then we would have to consider that seriously. But once again, actions speak louder than words. It is there in the economic statement.
What did the Government do regarding home insulation? It cut the Canadian home insulation program. That makes no sense in the present environment and it certainly leaves us with no justification for approving the borrowing request. From the perspective of investment or return on investment, Mr. Speaker, the Government's request falls short. It would be helpful, Mr. Speaker, if the Government would invest in the insulation of homes and the rehabilitation of older homes. There are many older homes across the country which are structurally sound. If a few dollars were spent on those homes, they could be brought up to par and would last for many more years. That would be a useful investment of public dollars.
Is there any reason for us to believe that the Government will be using the funds it wants us to approve today for such a worth-while purpose? Would it invest in the rehabilitation of older homes in the country? Its own economic statement tells us it will not Mr. Speaker. In that economic statement, the Government cut the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. It cut monies from public expenditures which would have allowed older homes to serve a useful purpose for a much longer period of time. From the perspective of investment, based on the Government's actions, since it will not give us any information on what it wants to use this money for, its request for approval of borrowing falls short.
Perhaps we could look at its request for borrowing from a different perspective. I will wrap up what I have to say, Mr. Speaker. We have had simply to speculate upon the possible uses to which the Government would put borrowed funds. A few short months ago that Party was in Opposition and it recognized the importance of the accountability of the executive to Parliament in the area of public spending. Now that that Party is in office, it has failed to recognize the basic truth. This is a severe disappointment and it will increase cynicism in the country.

One of the many cutbacks which took me by surprise, Mr. Speaker, is the one related to the Summer Canada Program which was set up by the Liberal government and which was a boon to thousands of young students. The Progressive Conservatives have described that program as a band-aid program.
Mr. Speaker, again I say to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) that it is not a band-aid program, if only because it does enable students throughout Canada to work during their summer holidays and earn a few dollars to help pay their tuition fees. It seems that nobody wants to hear anything about this Summer Canada Program. Earlier today, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) asked a question about the
Summer Canada Program, but the Prime Minister evaded the question neatly, and there was no meaningful answer, Mr. Speaker.
A few weeks ago I asked the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) whether he thought the Summer Canada Program was a band-aid program. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member himself did admit that it was nothing of the kind, and I fully agree with him.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, in the newspaper Le Droit last December 5, there was an article about the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) entitled 'Champagne avoids the real problems1, which said the following:
Minister Champagne, who is also coordinator of the activities surrounding National Youth Year 1985, has managed not to mention even once in her speech the problem of unemployment which affects 17.6 percent of our young people between the ages of 16 and 24.
"In fact, there was no mention of the real problems", as one of the students noted, Mr. Speaker.
I see that you want me to hurry up, Mr. Speaker.
In closing, I would like to mention that my main concern, is about the students who will want to work next summer. I therefore urge the Prime Minister, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the Minister of State for Youth, and also the Minister of Finance to do something for them.
Finally, I want to ask this Government to keep its promises, and I also want to say this to the ministers involved: "Please, reverse your stand and see to it that our students can find work!" As for the Government, it should be true to its commitment to provide prosperity for Canadians and jobs for those who want to work. These are some of the promises made by this Government, and in the interests of all Canadians, we sincerely hope that those promises will be kept, and you can be sure, Mr. Speaker, that we of the Official Opposition shall always support Government initiatives aimed at providing employment for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a good deal of pleasure to join in the debate this afternoon. Also I should like to join with other Hon. Members in congratulating you on your appointment. I am certain the House will run more smoothly and that high sticking will be kept to a minimum.
The Government proposes to borrow something in the order of $16 billion. It is interesting to sit in the House today with a kind of feeling of deja vu or a reverse of dej'a vu and to hear the screams and shouts from this side about borrowing without any plan or indication of what the borrowing will be used for. It is interesting to hear the ragged comments of the former opposition group which simply put down any necessity for giving the House of Commons and the taxpayers of Canada some indication of what it proposes to do with $16 billion. It is an amazing situation. Some of the open government about which those Members talked is complete nonsense in view of the comments they have made to date.
I should like to offer some suggestions in terms of spending that $16 billion. If they would simply keep their promises, that $16 billion would be adequate. A reminder of some of their promises might be useful. In my partiuclar area and along the entire coast of British Columbia, which now has a number of Tories representing it who made those same promises, the fishing industry is a disaster. The Conservative Government promised to spend $100 million in a buy-back program to assist fishermen who are in an extremely bad position. It was promised. The $16 billion could help deliver it. Why not keep some of the promises made by the Government during the election period? The Tories promised $200 million for Salmo-nid Enhancement Program. It would put thousands of people back to work on the coast of British Columbia, thousands of people who are financially flat on their backs and facing ruin. They recognize that problem. They made a promise to those people and now they are failing to keep it. The $16 billion of borrowing could be used for that. A firm, hard promise was made and nothing was delivered.
That same Party, campaigning for votes of the people in the forest industry who are suffering as badly, promised a $100 million reforestation program. It would create an enormous amount of employment on the coast of British Columbia. However, what do we hear from the Conservative Government? There has been absolute silence on that promise. We hear that the cupboard is bare.
Fishermen, loggers and others in the forest industry, have lost the opportunity of employment. They could be put back to work in the Salmonid Enhancement Program and in reforestation programs. Of course they could be assisted in the buyback program, it it ever comes to pass.
They also promised to revamp the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. People involved in the fishing industry on the coast of British Columbia in communities from Prince Rupert
Borrowing Authority
to Vancouver who are dependent upon fishing, as well as industries and small businesses which are dependent upon fishing, were promised that the Department of Fisheries would be revamped. That Department affects the lives of a great many people and many of the businesses there. They promised to make it more responsive to the people of that area. They promised to create an advisory committee. It was more than an advisory committee; the Conservatives called it a management committee comprised of representatives of the industry. What do we have right now? We have 1,200 public servants in the Department of Fisheries on the West Coast who have received no instructions from the Ministry in Ottawa. They have no instructions on what to do. There is a policy void out there. No one knows what is going on. Instead of revamping the Department or establishing a management committee, we have chaos out there right now. People are losing their vessels and their homes. They are unable to qualify for unemployment insurance. The prospect with a Conservative Government in place is that social assistance is the order of the day for those people.
If they want to borrow $16 billion, they can go ahead and do it. However, they should at least give us some indication of what will be done with that money. Why do they not keep their promises? The people along the coast of British Columbia would be a lot better off.
The fishing industry on the coast of B.C. is in serious trouble. The Government promised open government. A number of cabinet Ministers have said, "Our door is open; if you have a problem, raise it". I am somewhat confused because a number of major groups out there are having difficulty. They are in a policy vacuum. They know they have had an enormous number of hundred million dollar promises. All they received was $4.2 billion in cut-backs, as well as the $30 million in cuts in the Department of Fisheries to which my colleague referred. There is nothing for them. They will spend this winter, perhaps next spring and perhaps the next fishing season with nothing. By that time there will be nothing to make policy about because that industry on the coast of B.C. will be finished completely.
Turning to the buy-back program, it is critical that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) and the Government move now with assistance. People are losing their vessels. It was impossible for many people to earn income from fishing this year. It is a complete disaster because the Department of Fisheries and Oceans compressed the fishing season so much that very few people earned enough money to make their boat payments. Many people did not earn enough money to qualify for unemployment insurance. Income was at an extremely depressed level.
The Minister cannot sit here and do nothing. He must act quickly. This buy-back program was promised. It was on a scale of $100 million. It should have been under way this year. People should have an understanding of what will happen. The promise was made, it should be kept. Time is wasting and time is critical.
I should like to refer briefly to the management committee. The cut-back in fishing time has been a serious problem. The

Department of Fisheries has literally put many fishermen out of business. In the Johnstone Strait, communities such as Port Hardy, Alert Bay, Port McNeill, Campbell River and many others are dependent upon the fishery. They have been promised that it will continue to exist. However, the indication through the Department of Fisheries now is that that fishery is being compressed. Eventually it will be destroyed and they will be driven out. The gulf trollers, the people who work on the Straits of Georgia, were invited some years ago to take either an inside licence or an outside licence. Those who opted for the inside licence in the Gulf of Georgia were told that that fishery would continue and that they should have no fear of being put out of business.
Last season the Department of Fisheries and Oceans put them out of business. It limited their fishing season to a point where they could not earn enough income to provide a living. This virtually destroyed many people. They were told that the burden of conservation on chinook salmon was so important that everyone had to share. The gulf trollers were told that they could not fish on April 1, that they would have to start at almost the mid-point of the fishing season and that they would be shut down early. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans at that time said that the burden of conservation had to be shared, but it was not shared by the recreational fishery. There was a complete slaughter in the eyes of many people as the chinook salmon were simply reallocated from gulf trollers to the recreational fishery. Those fish never got to the spawning grounds.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans must make a statement indicating what will happen to gulf trollers who were told that they would continue to have a place in the fishing industry in the Province of British Columbia. It turns out that that is absolutely false.
The idea of open government is not coming to pass. We are seeing many important groups on the coast of British Columbia asking for meetings with the Minister. He does not have to make commitments to them. He simply has to give an indication that the door is open. Many groups want to meet with him including, we are given to understand, officials within his own Department who cannot get time. The Native Brotherhood of British Columbia would like to meet with him. Important Indian bands along the coast of B.C. would like to meet with him. United Fishermen and Allied Workers and other groups within the industry would like to meet with him, but there is no opportunity. His flacks are too efficient. They are saying, "Maybe next year". Maybe it will be some other time. Maybe it will be after there is no fishing industry. Open government does not exist. Anyone who thinks it does is extremely naive or a fool.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) had the courage to venture out to British Columbia with his officials. He met briefly with many groups under the responsibility of his Ministry. He attended the native brotherhood convention, an extremely important group on the coast of B.C. I urge the Minister of Fisheries to get his can out there and meet with these groups. He should at least
hear their problems and suggestions for solutions and then get on with the business of making the statements that will give them the opportunity to know where their lives are going. Where is this open government?
The Salmonid Enhancement Program is vitally important. We are watching the destruction of the fishing industry and the salmonid species on the coast of British Columbia. In some cases this is coming about as a result of overfishing and in other cases as a result of habitat destruction. We know that we have to get more involved in the process of salmonid enhancement. The program in that area was cut drastically by the previous Government. The present Government promised $200 million in salmonid enhancement funding. It must deliver on those funds. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The Right Hon. Prime Minister-
-too has expressed an understanding of the problems facing the tourism sector. The following quote from one of his speeches in Halifax during the campaign shows his concern. "A Progressive Conservative Government will recognize the importance of the tourism and travel industry to the Canadian economy in general and the Atlantic provinces in particular by implementing the following three-point program: As part of our proposed national conference on the economy, we will examine gasoline, alcohol, food and lodging taxes which are reducing the competitiveness of Canada's tourism industry".
We know the actions that have been undertaken by this Government. The price of gasoline has increased by nine cents a litre. The price of alcohol has increased by 1 per cent. The fares for ferry services in Atlantic Canada, a service that is vital to the tourism industry, will be increased substantially. Not only will the services in national parks be reduced, but it will cost more to use those facilities.

Mr. Speaker, it is a most deadly sin, in the sense that they knew very well what they were undertaking to do. Indeed, last spring the Opposition Members were continuously criticizing the Government about the price of gasoline. And in no less than 26 speeches did they oppose oil price increases. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, this is a sin because they knew very well what they were doing. I cannot trust a Government that acts in such a way.

In his economic and fiscal statement, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said, "We must have faith in ourselves and in our country". I agree with that. However, if we are to have faith in the Government, the Government must show it has some heart for the people, for faith comes from the heart. I cannot have faith in the Government because the Government has shown no feeling for Canadians.

This is why, Mr. Speaker, I cannot support the Bill as introduced, because the Government has not yet deserved my confidence, and I support the amendment to Bill C-l 1.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate for the first time, if for no other reason than to be of assistance, aid and comfort to the Government and to assist the Progressive Conservative Party.
The point we have been trying to make is not necessarily NDP policy. We are not asking for NDP programs to be implemented. We are asking the Government and Progressive Conservative Party Members to do what they demanded in Parliament all along and fought for, I must say to their credit, with some success. In the summer of 1982 they fought the government on a borrowing Bill on excellent grounds. We were pleased to support the Progressive Conservative Party in the summer of 1982 on this very same subject. We are only trying to be helpful. I do not understand why Conservative Members are not applauding our assistance. I do not understand why they cannot rise in the House and say that we have had enough of the old Liberal style of borrowing Bills drafted by the same old bureaucrats and that the new Government will put in place the changes it promised on September 4 by changing the way the Government requests borrowing. However, we are getting the same thing the Liberals gave us at least twice in the last few years.
There was strenuous opposition to the methods being used by the then Liberal government on the part of members of the Progressive Conservative Party and members of the New Democratic Party. In order to implement its own policies and remain true to the excellent battle it fought in June and July 1982, all the Conservative Government needs to do is what the opposition Parties succeeded in forcing the then Liberal Government into doing in 1982. It should delete S16 billion from this Bill, because that is the amount of money that is to be borrowed for the Fiscal year 1985-86 which does not begin until April 1.
I do not know of anyone who would ask to borrow money he or she would not need for another four and a half months. I do not know of anyone who would lend money to someone who asked for that. Why does the Government want to have the authority to borrow money at least four and a half months before it will need it?
I have been reading Hansard from 1982. I believe one of the best quotes in Hansard comes from the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). As reported on page 19454 of Hansard, he said:
That is an affront to this Parliament. No banker outside of these walls who deals with a businessman or businesswoman, large or small, would grant a line of credit to a financially crippled business that refuses to provide projections of its cash flows. No banker would do this, yet that is what this Government is asking the House of Commons to do.
The Government has not told us what its cash flows will be between now and the end of March and it certainly will not have the foggiest idea what those cash flows will be in the next fiscal year until a budget is brought in and the taxpayers know what the tax regimes will be. In any event, Hansard of those days makes excellent reading. It is the one time when most

December 5, 1984
Borrowing Authority
speeches made by Conservative Members were really worth reading.
I hope that Conservative Members appreciate that we are trying to be helpful to them. All we have done is to move the same motion that was moved by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead in July, 1982. I thought that that would be appreciated by my hon. friends in the Progressive Conservative Party.
We can support the borrowing of $5.3 billion for the rest of the fiscal year. We can even go along with the borrowing of $2 billion for a cushion to take care of any unforeseen happenings, whether it be an emergency with the Canadian dollar or emergency spending for other things that might occur between now and the end of March. We find that acceptable. However, to ask us to approve the borrowing of $ 16 billion before we are even into the next year, is, as the Right Hon. Member said in 1982, an affront to Parliament.
The Government is trying to cut the deficit. Of course, when it cuts the deficit, it increases unemployment. This means that deficit cutting is the Government's first priority, although "jobs, jobs, jobs" is a first priority as well. That outfit over there has more first priorities than any outfit I have ever seen.
I would like to quote the words of someone who is not a member of the NDP who supports the arguments we have made since this Parliament started. Dr. Harold Chorney is a professor at the University of Concordia and I like what he has said because I used words to the same effect during the Throne Speech debate. It is nice to see these words reiterated by an economist. My information reads:
Chorney's study says "the current debate about the deficit seems to ignore the lessons of the 1930s".
Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, how R.B. Bennett, Mackenzie King and that breed of cats from the 1930s harped at us, at Parliament and the people of Canada? It goes on:
Then, as now, the cry was to reduce deficits, restore "sound public finance" and let the private sector promote economic recovery. Then, as now, this policy was doomed to fail."
The current policy is doomed to fail just as the policy of the 1930s failed. If the Government wants to cut the deficit, it has to take measures which include additional borrowings starting now. If the Government can reduce the unemployment rate from 11.5 per cent to 7 per cent or 7.5 per cent, it can wipe out the $34 billion deficit over a period of three and a half years. That is all the Government need do. If it wants to get rid of the deficit, that is the route to go.
If the Government were to ask Parliament for borrowing authority in order to create jobs, put businessmen back into
business and workers back to work, these people would be paying income tax, and that would liquidate the borrowings. The Government would be accomplishing the objective that all of us in this House want. However, it has its priorities reversed.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister in charge of CMHC and other Ministers had completed an across-Canada survey of what housing projects are in the works that can be started sooner than otherwise planned, we could borrow now whatever our share of the cost would be. This could be done in order to advance programs, whether they be senior citizens' programs, co-operative programs, public programs or any private housing programs in which federal authorities may be involved. We could canvass all of the municipalities in Canada. We could ask what works are in progress that could be advanced and speeded up. We could borrow whatever money is required for the federal cost-sharing responsibility now and get those projects started.
If you could give me another 60 seconds, Mr. Speaker, I would call it six o'clock. I would be happy if you could do that.
